01_Mass_weight_and_gravitational_field_s.title: Mass, weight and gravitational field strength
01_Mass_weight_and_gravitational_field_s.subject: Physics

objectives.statement: Define mass and weight, use W = mg to calculate one quantity from the other, and recall that g is about 9.8 N/kg near the Earth's surface.
Explain weight as the effect of a gravitational field acting on mass, and connect gravitational field strength (in N/kg) to free-fall acceleration (in m/s²).

prerequisites.statement: Multiply and divide a decimal number by another decimal number and keep track of the unit attached to the result.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Every calculation in this lesson rearranges W = mg, which needs reliable decimal multiplication and division.

prerequisites.statement: Recall that a free-falling object near the Earth's surface speeds up by about 9.8 m/s every second.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: This lesson connects that acceleration value to the gravitational field strength used in W = mg, so the number should already feel familiar.

prerequisites.statement: Read a numerical value together with its unit from a labelled scale or display.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Telling mass and weight apart depends on reading the unit on a balance or a force meter correctly, not just the number.

diagnostic_items.question: A force meter reads 4.9 N. If the gravitational field strength is 9.8 N/kg, what is the mass that produces this reading? (Use mass = weight ÷ gravitational field strength.)

common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner copies the newton reading directly as a mass in kilograms, treating the two units as interchangeable.
The learner multiplies instead of dividing: $4.9\times9.8$.
The learner divides $9.8\div4.9$, inverting which number is the numerator.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: This checks whether the learner can rearrange and compute $m=W/g$ correctly before the lesson relies on it repeatedly.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Write $W=mg$ next to the question, circle the unknown, and rehearse the rearrangement with one further numeric example before continuing.

theory_blocks.title: The same block on Earth and on the Moon
theory_blocks.body:
Picture the same 10 kg block measured on Earth and then on the Moon. A beam balance, which compares the block with standard masses, would still read 10 kg in both places, because the block has not lost or gained any material by travelling there. A force meter, however, would show a much smaller reading on the Moon.

This difference is the whole point of separating mass from weight. [[blue:**Mass**]] is the amount of matter in an object, measured in kilograms, and it does not depend on where the object is. [[orange:**Weight**]] is the force that a gravitational field exerts on that mass, measured in newtons, and it is different wherever the field strength is different. The table below compares the same block in two locations.

assets.caption: The same 10 kg block on Earth and on the Moon: the mass reading stays the same, but the weight reading changes because the gravitational field strength is different.
assets.purpose: Make the mass/weight distinction concrete with a single consistent object compared across two locations, satisfying the unit's two-location comparison asset.

theory_blocks.title: Weight, mass and gravitational field strength: W = mg
theory_blocks.body:
Weight, mass and gravitational field strength are linked by

$$W = mg$$

where $W$ is the weight in newtons (N), $m$ is the mass in kilograms (kg), and $g$ is the gravitational field strength in newtons per kilogram (N/kg). Near the Earth's surface, $g\approx9.8\,\mathrm{N/kg}$, which means every kilogram of mass experiences about 9.8 N of gravitational force. Rearranged, $g=\dfrac{W}{m}$: gravitational field strength is defined as the gravitational force per unit mass.

For a 2.0 kg mass near the Earth's surface, $W=2.0\times9.8=19.6\,\mathrm{N}$. This relationship only describes the force due to gravity: it does not include friction, air resistance or any other force that might also act on the object.

theory_blocks.title: Two things not to assume
theory_blocks.body: Two slips are easy to make with this topic. First, $g\approx9.8\,\mathrm{N/kg}$ is the value to use in a calculation; [[orange:10 N/kg is only a convenient rounded estimate for a quick mental check]], and should not be substituted into a worked answer unless a question specifically asks for an estimate. Second, an object described as 'weightless' has not lost its mass: far out in space its weight may be tiny because the gravitational field there is very weak, and astronauts floating in an orbiting spacecraft still have weight (they float because they and the spacecraft are falling freely together), but in every case the matter making up the object, and therefore its mass, is unchanged.

theory_blocks.title: Gravitational field strength and free-fall acceleration
theory_blocks.body:
Gravitational field strength can also be written in units of metres per second squared (m/s²), because $1\,\mathrm{N/kg}=1\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$ once the units are expanded ($1\,\mathrm{N}=1\,\mathrm{kg\,m/s^2}$, so $1\,\mathrm{N/kg}=1\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$). This is why the number 9.8 appears twice in earlier work: once as the gravitational field strength, $g\approx9.8\,\mathrm{N/kg}$, and once as the free-fall acceleration of a falling object, $\approx9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$.

The two quantities describe the same physical effect from two angles: N/kg emphasises force per unit mass, while m/s² emphasises the acceleration that force produces on a freely falling object. They are always numerically equal (on the Moon, for example, both are about 1.6), but air resistance means a falling object does not always accelerate at exactly this rate in practice.

keywords.definition: The quantity of matter in an object, measured in kilograms; it does not depend on location.
The force exerted on an object's mass by a gravitational field, measured in newtons.
The force exerted per unit mass by a gravitational field; near the Earth's surface, $g\approx9.8\,\mathrm{N/kg}$.
The SI unit of force, including weight.

worked_examples.statement: **Finding a weight from a mass.** A bag of rice has a mass of 5.0 kg. Calculate its weight near the Earth's surface, taking $g=9.8\,\mathrm{N/kg}$.
worked_examples.interpretation: Check by dividing back: $49\div9.8=5.0\,\mathrm{kg}$, which matches the given mass.

worked_examples.statement: **Finding a mass from a weight.** An astronaut has a weight of 588 N while standing on Earth. Taking $g=9.8\,\mathrm{N/kg}$, calculate the astronaut's mass.
reasoning: The reading is in newtons, so it is a weight, not a mass.
worked_examples.interpretation: Check by multiplying back: $60\times9.8=588\,\mathrm{N}$, which matches the given weight.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Writing the mass as 588 kg, as if the newton reading could simply be relabelled in kilograms.

worked_examples.statement: **Comparing two locations.** A rock has a mass of 12 kg. Calculate its weight near the Earth's surface ($g\approx9.8\,\mathrm{N/kg}$) and on the Moon ($g\approx1.6\,\mathrm{N/kg}$), and explain what stays the same between the two calculations and what changes.
reasoning: The mass of the rock, 12 kg, is the same number in both calculations because mass does not depend on location.
Only the gravitational field strength $g$ changes between the two calculations.
worked_examples.interpretation: The rock's mass, 12 kg, is identical in both calculations; its weight is about six times smaller on the Moon, because the Moon's gravitational field strength is about six times smaller than the Earth's.

worked_examples.statement: **A two-step, two-location problem.** On Earth, an item of equipment has a weight of 686 N ($g=9.8\,\mathrm{N/kg}$). (a) Calculate its mass. (b) Calculate its weight on a planet where $g=3.7\,\mathrm{N/kg}$.
reasoning: Part (a) gives a weight and asks for a mass, so rearrange $W=mg$ to $m=W/g$ first.
Part (b) then reuses that same mass, because mass does not change between locations, with the new value of $g$.
worked_examples.interpretation: Check (a) by multiplying back: $70\times9.8=686\,\mathrm{N}$. The mass of 70 kg found in (a) is exactly the mass that is reused, unchanged, in (b).

guided_exercises.statement: A box has a mass of 6.0 kg. Calculate its weight near the Earth's surface, taking $g=9.8\,\mathrm{N/kg}$.
hints: Identify which quantity is already given: is it a mass or a weight?
Use $W=mg$ with $g=9.8\,\mathrm{N/kg}$.
Check your answer by dividing it back by $g$.
common_errors: Writing the answer as 60 N by rounding $g$ up to 10 N/kg before multiplying.
guided_exercises.full_solution:
**Step 1 — Identify:** Identify which quantity is already given: is it a mass or a weight?

**Step 2 — Method:** Use $W=mg$ with $g=9.8\,\mathrm{N/kg}$.

**Step 3 — Calculate:** $W=6.0\times9.8=58.8\,\mathrm{N}$. Check: $58.8\div9.8=6.0\,\mathrm{kg}$.

**Step 4 — Check:** Check your answer by dividing it back by $g$.

guided_exercises.statement: A spring balance reads 24.5 N when a stone hangs from it near the Earth's surface. Calculate the mass of the stone.
hints: A spring balance reading in newtons measures weight, not mass.
Rearrange $W=mg$ to make $m$ the unknown.
Check your answer by multiplying it by $g$.
common_errors: Reporting 24.5 kg, treating the newton reading directly as a mass in kilograms.
guided_exercises.full_solution:
**Step 1 — Identify:** A spring balance reading in newtons measures weight, not mass.

**Step 2 — Method:** Rearrange $W=mg$ to make $m$ the unknown.

**Step 3 — Calculate:** $m=24.5\div9.8=2.5\,\mathrm{kg}$. Check: $2.5\times9.8=24.5\,\mathrm{N}$.

**Step 4 — Check:** Check your answer by multiplying it by $g$.

exercises.statement: State whether each of the following is a measurement of mass or of weight, and give the correct unit for each: (a) a reading of 500 g on a kitchen balance; (b) a reading of 4.9 N on a spring balance; (c) a reading of 12 on a bathroom scale calibrated in kilograms.
exercises.answer: (a) Mass, in grams. (b) Weight, in newtons. (c) Mass, in kilograms.
exercises.full_solution: A bathroom scale is designed and calibrated to display mass directly, in kilograms, even though the mechanism inside responds to the weight pressing down on it.
common_errors: Calling the spring-balance reading in (b) a mass because a number on a dial 'feels' like a measurement, regardless of its unit.

exercises.statement: A suitcase has a mass of 18 kg. Calculate its weight near the Earth's surface, taking $g=9.8\,\mathrm{N/kg}$.
exercises.full_solution: Check: $176.4\div9.8=18\,\mathrm{kg}$, which matches the given mass.
common_errors: Giving the answer as 180 N by rounding $g$ to 10 N/kg.

exercises.statement: A force meter shows a reading of 3.92 N for a small object near the Earth's surface. Calculate the object's mass, taking $g=9.8\,\mathrm{N/kg}$.
exercises.full_solution: Check: $0.40\times9.8=3.92\,\mathrm{N}$, which matches the given reading.
common_errors: Multiplying 3.92 by 9.8 instead of dividing, giving a much larger and physically unreasonable mass.

exercises.statement: A probe's weight on Earth is 980 N, where $g=9.8\,\mathrm{N/kg}$. (a) Calculate the probe's mass. (b) The probe then lands on a small moon where $g=2.0\,\mathrm{N/kg}$. Calculate its weight there.
exercises.full_solution: Check (a): $100\times9.8=980\,\mathrm{N}$. The mass of 100 kg found in (a) is the same mass reused in (b); only the gravitational field strength changes.
common_errors: Recalculating a new mass for the small moon, as if mass depended on the local field strength in the same way that weight does.

exam_questions.statement: A trolley has a mass of 4.0 kg. (a) Calculate its weight near the Earth's surface, taking $g=9.8\,\mathrm{N/kg}$. (b) The trolley is taken to a region of space where the gravitational field strength is 3.7 N/kg. State its mass there, and calculate its new weight.
mark_scheme: Uses $W=mg$ with correct substitution for part (a).
States $39.2\,\mathrm{N}$, with the unit, for part (a).
States that the mass is unchanged at 4.0 kg in the new location.
Uses $W=mg$ with the new field strength for part (b).
States $14.8\,\mathrm{N}$, with the unit, for part (b).

exam_questions.statement: Explain, in terms of a gravitational field, why an object's weight can change when it is moved to a different location while its mass stays the same.
exam_questions.answer: Mass measures the amount of matter in the object, which does not depend on where the object is. Weight is the force exerted on that mass by the local gravitational field. Different locations, such as the Earth and the Moon, have different gravitational field strengths, so the same mass experiences a different force, $W=mg$, in each place.
mark_scheme: States that mass is the amount of matter in the object and does not depend on location.
States that weight is the force exerted on the mass by the local gravitational field.
States that different locations have different gravitational field strengths.
Links the two ideas using $W=mg$ to explain why the weight changes while the mass does not.

challenge_questions.statement: A 3.0 kg mass is hung from a force meter on the surface of another planet, and the meter reads 11.1 N. (a) Calculate the gravitational field strength at the planet's surface. (b) State the acceleration of free fall at that surface, with its unit. (c) Explain why the two answers have the same numerical value.
hints: Rearrange $W=mg$ to make $g$ the subject: the field strength is the gravitational force on each kilogram.
Write the newton in base units: $1\,\mathrm{N}=1\,\mathrm{kg\,m/s^2}$, so $1\,\mathrm{N/kg}=1\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$.
In free fall the only force acting on the object is its own weight, so the force per kilogram is also the acceleration produced.
challenge_questions.answer: (a) $g=\dfrac{W}{m}=\dfrac{11.1}{3.0}=3.7\,\mathrm{N/kg}$. (b) The acceleration of free fall is $3.7\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$. (c) Gravitational field strength is the gravitational force per unit mass. For an object in free fall the weight is the only force acting, so every kilogram of the object is given an acceleration equal to that force per kilogram. Because $1\,\mathrm{N/kg}=1\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$, the field strength in N/kg and the acceleration of free fall in m/s² are always numerically equal.
challenge_questions.full_solution: Check: $3.0\times3.7=11.1\,\mathrm{N}$, which matches the force-meter reading. The value 3.7 N/kg is close to the gravitational field strength at the surface of Mars, so this planet's field is roughly 38 % as strong as the Earth's 9.8 N/kg.
common_errors: Multiplying instead of dividing, $11.1\times3.0=33.3$, which gives a field strength stronger than the Earth's for a reading smaller than the weight the same mass would have on Earth.
Writing 9.8 m/s² for part (b) out of habit: the acceleration of free fall takes the local value of $g$, and this planet is not the Earth.

mcq.stem: A bag of sugar has a mass of 2.0 kg. Calculate its weight near the Earth's surface, taking $g=9.8\,\mathrm{N/kg}$.

options.why_wrong: this restates the mass value with the wrong unit, treating mass and weight as the same quantity.
this adds $g$ to the mass ($2.0+9.8$) instead of multiplying them.
this rounds $g$ up to 10 N/kg instead of using the correct value of 9.8 N/kg.

mcq.stem: An astronaut has a weight of 686 N while standing on Earth, where $g=9.8\,\mathrm{N/kg}$. What is the astronaut's mass?

options.why_wrong: this treats the newton reading as if it were already a mass given in kilograms.
this multiplies 686 by 9.8 instead of dividing.
this uses $g=10\,\mathrm{N/kg}$ instead of the more accurate value of 9.8 N/kg.

mcq.stem: A rock has a mass of 12 kg, and its weight on the Moon, where $g\approx1.6\,\mathrm{N/kg}$, is about 19.2 N. What is its weight on Earth, where $g\approx9.8\,\mathrm{N/kg}$?

options.why_wrong: this repeats the Moon weight, as if weight did not change between locations.
this reports the mass number with the wrong unit, confusing mass with weight.
this reports the Moon's gravitational field strength itself, not a calculated weight.

mcq.stem: A 5.0 kg block is taken from the Earth's surface ($g\approx9.8\,\mathrm{N/kg}$) to the Moon's surface ($g\approx1.6\,\mathrm{N/kg}$). Which statement is correct?

options.text: Both its mass and its weight become smaller on the Moon.
options.why_wrong: mass is a property of the amount of matter in the block and does not depend on the local gravitational field strength.

options.text: Its mass becomes smaller but its weight stays the same.
options.why_wrong: this reverses which quantity actually depends on gravitational field strength.

options.text: Both its mass and its weight stay exactly the same on both worlds.
options.why_wrong: weight is a force produced by the gravitational field, and the Moon's field strength is different from the Earth's.

options.text: Its mass stays at 5.0 kg on both worlds; only its weight changes.

mcq.explanation: Mass measures the amount of matter and is unaffected by location; weight equals $mg$, and $g$ is different on the Moon, so only the weight changes.

mcq.stem: Gravitational field strength $g$ at a point is defined as which of the following?

options.text: The gravitational force per unit mass at that point
The gravitational force acting on the object at that point
options.why_wrong: this is the object's weight, which gets larger for a larger mass; the field strength is the force on each kilogram, so it does not depend on the object placed there.

options.text: The mass per unit gravitational force at that point
options.why_wrong: this inverts the ratio; such a quantity would be measured in kg/N, not in N/kg.

options.text: The gravitational force per unit volume at that point
options.why_wrong: volume plays no part in $W=mg$; the field strength relates the gravitational force to the mass, not to the space the object occupies.

mcq.explanation: Gravitational field strength is defined as the gravitational force per unit mass, $g=\dfrac{W}{m}$, measured in N/kg. Near the Earth's surface $g\approx9.8\,\mathrm{N/kg}$, meaning each kilogram of mass experiences about 9.8 N.

flashcards.back: The amount of matter in an object, measured in kilograms (kg); it does not change with location.
The force exerted on an object's mass by a gravitational field, measured in newtons (N); it depends on the local gravitational field strength.

flashcards.front: What equation links weight, mass and gravitational field strength?
flashcards.back: $W=mg$, where $W$ is in newtons, $m$ is in kilograms and $g$ is in N/kg.

flashcards.front: How do mass and weight differ when an object moves from Earth to the Moon?
flashcards.back: Mass stays the same, because the amount of matter is unchanged. Weight becomes smaller, because the Moon's gravitational field strength (about 1.6 N/kg) is less than the Earth's (about 9.8 N/kg).

flashcards.front: Is the gravitational field strength g always exactly 10 N/kg?
flashcards.back: No. Near the Earth's surface $g\approx9.8\,\mathrm{N/kg}$; 10 N/kg is only a rough estimate for a quick mental check, not the accurate value to use in a calculation.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Mass and weight are just two different names for the same quantity.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Everyday speech uses 'weight' for both, and a kitchen scale is often read in kilograms even though the instrument inside responds to a force.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner answers a weight question in kilograms, or a mass question in newtons, without noticing the unit mismatch.
misconceptions.correct_model: Mass is the amount of matter in an object, in kilograms, and does not depend on location. Weight is the gravitational force on that mass, in newtons, and changes if the gravitational field strength changes.
misconceptions.remediation: Ask which unit the answer should have before calculating anything, then check the final unit matches that choice.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: An object that has no weight also has no mass.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Videos of astronauts floating are described as 'weightless', and the learner assumes nothing physical remains if nothing is pulling on it.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner states that mass 'disappears' or becomes zero wherever weight is zero.
misconceptions.correct_model: Weight depends on the local gravitational field strength, which can be very small far out in space (astronauts floating in orbit still have weight: they float because they are in free fall with their spacecraft); mass is a property of the object itself and stays the same regardless of the field around it.
misconceptions.remediation: Separate the two questions explicitly: how much matter is in the object (mass), and how strongly does the local field pull on it (weight)? Answer each one on its own.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: The gravitational field strength g is always exactly 10 N/kg.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: 10 N/kg is a convenient rounded value used for quick mental estimates, and learners often remember the rounded figure as if it were exact.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner uses g = 10 N/kg in a calculation after being given, or after recalling, the more accurate value of 9.8 N/kg.
misconceptions.correct_model: Near the Earth's surface, the gravitational field strength is about 9.8 N/kg; 10 N/kg is only a rough estimate for a quick check, not the value to use in a worked calculation.
misconceptions.remediation: Compare an answer calculated with g = 9.8 N/kg against the same calculation with g = 10 N/kg, and discuss why the two differ slightly.

common_mistakes.mistake: Treating a kilogram reading and a newton reading as the same kind of quantity.
common_mistakes.why: Mass and weight have different units because they measure different things: how much matter is present, and how strongly gravity pulls on it.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Check the unit before using a number in a calculation: kg means mass, N means weight.

common_mistakes.why: 10 N/kg is a rounded estimate used for quick mental checks, not the accurate value.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Use $g=9.8\,\mathrm{N/kg}$ near the Earth's surface unless a question explicitly gives a different value.

common_mistakes.mistake: Believing an object with no measured weight also has no mass.
common_mistakes.why: Weight depends on the local gravitational field strength, which can be very small, while mass is a property of the matter in the object itself.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Answer the mass question and the weight question separately: how much matter is there, and how strong is the local field pulling on it?

common_mistakes.mistake: Dividing by $g$ instead of multiplying, or the reverse, when rearranging $W=mg$.
common_mistakes.why: Rearranging the wrong way produces an answer that is far too large or far too small, and sometimes with the wrong unit.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Write down which quantity is unknown before rearranging: multiply mass by $g$ to find weight, divide weight by $g$ to find mass.

exam_notes: State clearly whether a question is asking about mass or weight before choosing which calculation to do.
Always give the correct unit: kilograms for mass, newtons for weight.
Use $g=9.8\,\mathrm{N/kg}$ unless the question gives a different value for a different location.
When asked to explain a change in weight, mention both the unchanged mass and the different gravitational field strength.

summary.big_idea: A gravitational field acts on an object's mass to produce its weight, so mass and weight have different units and can change differently.
key_points: Mass is the amount of matter in an object (kg); weight is the gravitational force on that mass (N).
Moving an object to a location with a different gravitational field strength changes its weight but never its mass.
Gravitational field strength (N/kg) and free-fall acceleration (m/s²) are the same physical quantity expressed in two equivalent units.
summary.what_to_remember_if_nothing_else: Mass never changes with location; weight does, because weight is mass multiplied by the local gravitational field strength.

02_Measuring_density.json.title: Measuring density
02_Measuring_density.json.subject: Physics

objectives.statement: Define density as mass divided by volume, and calculate density with consistent units (g/cm³ or kg/m³).

Measure the density of a liquid, a regular solid and a sinking irregular solid, using the correct mass and volume method for each, including subtracting an empty-container mass and checking for complete submersion.

prerequisites.statement: Measure a mass in grams or kilograms using a balance (from the previous lesson on mass and weight).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Every density calculation in this lesson starts from a correctly measured mass.

prerequisites.statement: Calculate the volume of a rectangular block as length times width times height, keeping the units consistent.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: The regular-solid method in this lesson needs this volume calculation before density can be found.

prerequisites.statement: Read a numbered scale, including finding the difference between an initial reading and a later reading.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: All three density methods in this lesson depend on reading a scale correctly and, for two of them, subtracting two readings rather than using just one.

diagnostic_items.question: A rectangular block measures 3.0 cm long, 2.0 cm wide and 1.5 cm high. Calculate its volume, and give the unit.

common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner adds the three dimensions, $3.0+2.0+1.5$, instead of multiplying them.
The learner multiplies only two of the dimensions, $3.0\times2.0$, and forgets the height.
The learner multiplies correctly but labels the result as an area, so the unit will not match the mass unit in a density calculation.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: This checks whether the learner can turn three measured lengths into a volume in cm³ before the regular-solid method relies on it.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Sketch the block, label the three dimensions, and say aloud that multiplying three lengths gives a cubic unit; then repeat with one further block, for example 4.0 cm × 2.5 cm × 2.0 cm, giving 20 cm³.

diagnostic_items.question: The water in a measuring cylinder stands at the 25.0 cm³ mark. More water is poured in and the reading becomes 34.5 cm³. By how much has the volume reading increased?

common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner quotes the final reading instead of the change, ignoring the water that was already in the cylinder.
The learner adds the two readings instead of subtracting one from the other.
The learner reads each level only to the nearest labelled mark, 25 and 35, instead of reading the half-division at 34.5.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: This checks whether the learner reads a cylinder scale precisely and finds a change as final reading minus initial reading, which two of the three density methods in this lesson depend on.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Point at both levels on a real or drawn cylinder, work out the value of one small division, and rehearse 'change = final − initial' on one further pair of readings, for example 18.0 cm³ rising to 23.5 cm³, giving 5.5 cm³.

theory_blocks.title: Same material, different size, same density
theory_blocks.body:
Imagine two cubes made of the same plastic material: a small cube of side 2 cm, and a larger cube of side 4 cm. The small cube has a volume of $2^3=8\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ and a mass of 16 g, so $16\div8=2.0\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}$. The larger cube has a volume of $4^3=64\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ and a mass of 128 g, so $128\div64=2.0\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}$ as well.

Both cubes give exactly the same answer, even though one has eight times the mass and eight times the volume of the other. This is the whole idea behind density: it is not a measure of how big or how heavy an object is, but of [[blue:how tightly packed its matter is]], mass for each unit of volume, and that packing is a property of the material, not of the particular lump of it being measured.

theory_blocks.title: Density: mass per unit volume
theory_blocks.body:
Density is defined as

$$\rho=\frac{m}{V}$$

where $\rho$ (density) is usually given in $\mathrm{g/cm^3}$ or $\mathrm{kg/m^3}$, $m$ (mass) is in grams or kilograms to match, and $V$ (volume) is in $\mathrm{cm^3}$ or $\mathrm{m^3}$ to match. The two unit pairs describe the same physical quantity and convert using $1\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}=1000\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}$, since one gram in one cubic centimetre is the same packing of matter as one thousand kilograms in one cubic metre.

This formula only gives a meaningful answer when the mass and the volume both belong to the same object. Mixing up the mass of one thing with the volume of something else, such as a container, produces a number that is not the material's density at all.

theory_blocks.title: Three ways to find a volume
theory_blocks.body: The method used to find a volume depends on what is being measured. A liquid takes the shape of its container, so its volume is read directly from a measuring cylinder's scale (its mass is found separately, by weighing the cylinder empty and then with the liquid, and subtracting). A regular solid, such as a rectangular block, has a volume that can be calculated from its measured dimensions. An irregular solid that sinks has no simple shape to measure, so its volume is instead found from the water (or another liquid) that it displaces when fully submerged.

assets.caption: Three ways to find a volume: subtract the empty-container mass for a liquid, measure the dimensions of a regular solid, and record the rise in level when an irregular solid that sinks is fully submerged.
assets.purpose: Show all three measurement methods side by side with realistic, internally consistent scale readings, satisfying the unit's three-method measurement diagram asset.

theory_blocks.title: Measuring the density of a liquid
theory_blocks.body:
First weigh the empty measuring cylinder and record its mass. Pour in the liquid sample, weigh the cylinder again, and subtract the empty-cylinder mass from this second reading: the difference is the mass of the liquid alone. Read the liquid's volume directly from the cylinder's scale, at eye level with the bottom of the meniscus. Finally, calculate $\rho=m/V$ using the liquid's mass and its volume.

Skipping the subtraction step is the most common source of error here: using the combined mass of the cylinder and the liquid, instead of the liquid's mass alone, gives a density that is far too high.

theory_blocks.title: Measuring the density of a regular solid
theory_blocks.body:
Measure the solid's dimensions with a ruler, and calculate its volume from its shape, for example length $\times$ width $\times$ height for a rectangular block. Weigh the solid on a balance to find its mass. Then calculate $\rho=m/V$.

Keep every length measurement in the same unit before multiplying them together, and keep the final volume in a unit, such as cm³, that matches the unit used for the mass.

theory_blocks.title: Measuring the density of a sinking irregular solid (displacement)
theory_blocks.body: Partly fill a measuring cylinder with water and record the volume reading. Lower the solid in gently, using a thread if needed so it does not splash water out, until it is completely covered by the water. Record the new, higher volume reading. The solid's volume is the rise in the reading, final reading minus initial reading, not the final reading on its own. Weigh the solid separately on a balance to find its mass, then calculate $\rho=m/V$.

theory_blocks.title: Why complete submersion matters
theory_blocks.body: The displacement method only gives the true volume of the solid if two conditions are met: the solid must be [[blue:**completely submerged**]], with no part sticking out above the water surface, and there must be [[blue:**no trapped air bubbles**]] clinging to its surface. If the solid is only partly submerged, the rise in the reading will be smaller than the solid's actual volume, and the calculated density will come out too high. If an air bubble is trapped against the solid, the measured rise will be too large, including the bubble's volume as if it were part of the solid, and the calculated density will come out too low.

keywords.definition: Mass per unit volume of a substance, usually expressed in g/cm³ or kg/m³.
A way of finding the volume of an irregular solid from the rise in liquid level it causes when fully submerged.
The curved surface of a liquid in a container, read at eye level for an accurate volume.
A solid with a simple geometric shape whose volume can be calculated directly from its measured dimensions.

worked_examples.statement: **Finding the density of a liquid.** An empty measuring cylinder has a mass of 25.0 g. With a sample of oil poured in, the cylinder and oil together have a mass of 125.0 g, and the oil's volume, read from the cylinder's scale, is 80 cm³. Find the density of the oil.
reasoning: Subtract the empty-cylinder mass from the combined mass to isolate the oil's own mass.
Divide that mass by the oil's volume to find its density.
worked_examples.interpretation: Check: $1.25\times80=100.0\,\mathrm{g}$, which matches the oil's mass found above.

worked_examples.statement: **Finding the density of a regular solid.** A rectangular metal block measures 4.0 cm by 2.0 cm by 1.5 cm and has a mass of 94.8 g. Find its density.
worked_examples.interpretation: Check: $7.9\times12.0=94.8\,\mathrm{g}$, which matches the given mass.

worked_examples.statement: **Finding the density of an irregular solid that sinks.** A small stone is lowered into a measuring cylinder of water. The water level rises from 30 cm³ to 50 cm³, and the stone has a mass of 54 g. Find the stone's density, and explain why the stone must be completely covered by water for this method to work.
reasoning: The stone's volume is the rise in the reading, not the final reading on its own.
If the stone were only partly submerged, the rise in the reading would be smaller than the stone's true volume.
worked_examples.interpretation: Check: $2.7\times20=54\,\mathrm{g}$. If the stone were only partly submerged, the measured rise would be smaller than 20 cm³, and dividing the same 54 g by a smaller volume would give a density higher than the stone's true value.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Using the final reading of 50 cm³ alone as the stone's volume, instead of the rise in the reading.

worked_examples.statement: **Choosing a method and converting units.** An irregularly shaped lump of an unknown solid sinks in water. Describe a suitable method to find its density, then calculate the density in kg/m³ if the lump has a mass of 136 g and raises a measuring cylinder's reading from 40 cm³ to 60 cm³.
reasoning: Since the lump is irregular and sinks, the displacement method is the appropriate one, not direct measurement of its dimensions.
Find the volume from the rise in the cylinder reading, then combine it with the given mass.
Convert the resulting density from g/cm³ to kg/m³ by multiplying by 1000.
worked_examples.interpretation: Check: $6.8\times20=136\,\mathrm{g}$, matching the given mass, and $6.8\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}=6800\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}$ since $1\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}=1000\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}$.

guided_exercises.statement: A measuring cylinder containing water reads 35 cm³. After a metal nut is lowered in and fully covered by the water, the reading rises to 42 cm³. The nut has a mass of 54.6 g. Calculate the density of the metal.
hints: The nut's volume is the rise in the reading, not the final reading alone.
Subtract the initial reading from the final reading to find the volume.
Use density = mass ÷ volume, keeping cm³ and g together.
common_errors: Using 42 cm³ alone as the nut's volume, instead of the rise in the reading.
guided_exercises.full_solution:
**Step 1 — Identify:** The nut's volume is the rise in the reading, not the final reading alone.

**Step 2 — Method:** Subtract the initial reading from the final reading to find the volume.

**Step 3 — Calculate:** $V=42-35=7\,\mathrm{cm^3}$. $\rho=54.6\div7=7.8\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}$.

**Step 4 — Check:** Use density = mass ÷ volume, keeping cm³ and g together.

guided_exercises.statement: An empty beaker has a mass of 48.0 g. When filled with 60 cm³ of a salt solution, the beaker and solution together have a mass of 123.0 g. Calculate the density of the salt solution.
hints: Subtract the empty-container mass before dividing by the volume.
Keep the volume in cm³ to match the mass in grams.
Check your answer by multiplying it back by the volume.
common_errors: Dividing the full 123.0 g by 60 cm³ without subtracting the empty beaker's mass first.
guided_exercises.full_solution:
**Step 1 — Identify:** Subtract the empty-container mass before dividing by the volume.

**Step 2 — Method:** Keep the volume in cm³ to match the mass in grams.

**Step 3 — Calculate:** $m_{\text{liquid}}=123.0-48.0=75.0\,\mathrm{g}$. $\rho=75.0\div60=1.25\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}$.

**Step 4 — Check:** Check your answer by multiplying it back by the volume.

exercises.statement: A rectangular wooden block measures 5.0 cm by 4.0 cm by 2.0 cm and has a mass of 64.0 g. Calculate its density.

A technician has three unlabelled samples: a liquid, a regularly shaped solid block, and an irregularly shaped solid that sinks in water. For each sample, state which readings must be taken and how its volume would be found.
exercises.answer: Liquid: weigh the empty container, add the liquid and weigh again (subtract to find its mass), and read its volume directly from a measuring cylinder's scale. Regular solid: measure its dimensions with a ruler and calculate the volume from its shape; weigh it separately for its mass. Irregular solid that sinks: lower it, fully submerged, into a measuring cylinder of water and take the rise in the reading as its volume; weigh it separately for its mass.
common_errors: Reading the irregular solid's volume as the final cylinder reading on its own, instead of the rise in the reading.

exercises.statement: A sample has a mass of 0.154 kg and a volume of 200 cm³. Calculate its density in g/cm³.
exercises.full_solution: Converting the mass to grams first keeps both quantities in matching units before dividing.
common_errors: Dividing 0.154 by 200 without converting the mass to grams, giving an answer 1000 times too small.

exercises.statement: An engineer measures a metal component's density as 8.9 g/cm³ using a displacement method. Convert this density to kg/m³, and explain why using the measuring cylinder's total capacity, instead of the rise in its reading, would have given a wrong answer.
exercises.answer: $8.9\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}=8900\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}$ (multiplying by 1000, since $1\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}=1000\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}$). Using the cylinder's total capacity would include empty space that the component never occupied, giving too large a volume and therefore a density that is too small.
common_errors: Dividing by 1000 instead of multiplying when converting g/cm³ to kg/m³.

exam_questions.statement: A student finds the density of a liquid using a measuring cylinder and a balance. Describe a method for doing this, including how the mass of the liquid alone is found.
exam_questions.answer: Weigh the empty measuring cylinder and record its mass. Pour in the liquid and weigh the cylinder again. Subtract the empty-cylinder mass from this second reading to find the mass of the liquid alone. Read the liquid's volume directly from the cylinder's scale, at eye level with the bottom of the meniscus. Calculate density as the liquid's mass divided by its volume.
mark_scheme: States that the empty cylinder is weighed first.
States that the cylinder is weighed again with the liquid added.
States that the empty-cylinder mass is subtracted to find the liquid's mass alone.
States that density is calculated as mass divided by volume, with the volume read from the cylinder's scale.

exam_questions.statement: An irregular solid that sinks in water is lowered into a measuring cylinder. The water level rises from 42 cm³ to 66 cm³, and the solid has a mass of 43.2 g. (a) Calculate the solid's density. (b) State two precautions needed for this method to give an accurate volume.
exam_questions.answer: (a) $V=66-42=24\,\mathrm{cm^3}$; $\rho=43.2\div24=1.8\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}$. (b) The solid must be completely submerged, with no part above the water surface, and there must be no trapped air bubbles clinging to it.
mark_scheme: Finds the volume as the rise in the reading: $66-42=24\,\mathrm{cm^3}$.
Uses density = mass ÷ volume, $43.2\div24$ (M1); $=1.8\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}$, with the correct unit (A1).
States that the solid must be completely submerged.
States that there must be no trapped air bubbles against the solid.

challenge_questions.statement: An alloy block is made from two metals bonded together: 60 cm³ of metal A, which has a density of 8.0 g/cm³, and 40 cm³ of metal B, which has a density of 2.7 g/cm³. Calculate the overall density of the whole block.
hints: Find the mass of each metal separately, using mass = density × volume for each one.
Add the two masses together, and add the two volumes together.
Divide the total mass by the total volume to find the block's overall density.
challenge_questions.answer: Mass of A $=60\times8.0=480\,\mathrm{g}$. Mass of B $=40\times2.7=108\,\mathrm{g}$. Total mass $=480+108=588\,\mathrm{g}$; total volume $=60+40=100\,\mathrm{cm^3}$. Overall density $=588\div100=5.88\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}$.
challenge_questions.full_solution: This value lies between the densities of the two metals, which makes physical sense: the block is denser than metal B alone but less dense than metal A alone, because it is a mixture of the two.
common_errors: Averaging the two densities directly, $(8.0+2.7)/2=5.35\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}$, which ignores that the two metals occupy different volumes.

mcq.stem: An empty measuring cylinder has a mass of 30.0 g. With a liquid sample added, the total mass is 110.0 g, and the liquid's volume is 100 cm³. What is the density of the liquid?

options.why_wrong: this divides the full mass of 110.0 g by the volume, without subtracting the empty cylinder's mass first.
this adds the empty-cylinder mass instead of subtracting it.
this uses only the empty cylinder's mass of 30.0 g, ignoring the liquid that was added.

mcq.stem: An irregular solid is lowered into a measuring cylinder of water. The reading rises from 24 cm³ to 34 cm³. Which statement about the solid's volume is correct?

options.text: Its volume is 34 cm³, the final reading.
options.why_wrong: this ignores the 24 cm³ of water that was already in the cylinder before the solid was added.

options.text: Its volume is 24 cm³, the initial reading.
options.why_wrong: this uses the reading taken before the solid was even added to the cylinder.

options.text: Its volume is 10 cm³, the rise in the reading.
Its volume cannot be found without also weighing the displaced water.
options.why_wrong: the volume is found directly from the change in the cylinder's scale reading; no extra weighing is needed to find a volume this way.

mcq.explanation: The solid's volume is the rise in the reading: $34-24=10\,\mathrm{cm^3}$.

mcq.stem: A cube of side 3.0 cm has a mass of 54 g. A second cube, made of the same material, has a side of 6.0 cm. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The second cube has double the density because it is twice as wide.
options.why_wrong: density depends on the material, not on size; doubling every side length multiplies the volume by eight, not the density.

options.text: The second cube has a mass of 108 g, double the first cube's mass.
options.why_wrong: this doubles the mass in line with the side length, but mass scales with volume, which increases by a factor of eight, not two.

options.text: The second cube's density cannot be found without weighing it.
options.why_wrong: since both cubes are the same material, the density found from the first cube already applies to the second; only its volume or mass is needed to use it.

options.text: The second cube has the same density, 2.0 g/cm³, but a mass of 432 g.

mcq.explanation: First cube: $V=3.0^3=27\,\mathrm{cm^3}$, $\rho=54\div27=2.0\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}$. Second cube: $V=6.0^3=216\,\mathrm{cm^3}$, so its mass is $216\times2.0=432\,\mathrm{g}$, at the same density of 2.0 g/cm³.

mcq.stem: Which pair of units could both correctly express a density?

options.why_wrong: cm³/g is the inverse of density (volume per unit mass), not another way of expressing density itself.
N/kg is the unit of gravitational field strength, not density.
kg alone is a unit of mass; it carries no information about volume, so it cannot express a density.

mcq.explanation: g/cm³ and kg/m³ both give mass per unit volume, and they convert into each other using $1\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}=1000\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}$.

flashcards.back: Mass per unit volume, usually in g/cm³ or kg/m³.
$\rho=m/V$, with mass and volume measured in matching units.

flashcards.front: Does a bigger object always have a bigger density?
flashcards.back: No. Density depends on how tightly packed the material is, mass for each unit of volume, not on the size of the particular object.

flashcards.front: How is the mass of a liquid alone found, separately from its container?
flashcards.back: Weigh the empty container, then weigh the container with the liquid in it, and subtract the empty-container mass from the second reading.

flashcards.front: How does finding the volume of a regular solid differ from finding the volume of a sinking irregular solid?
flashcards.back: A regular solid's volume is calculated from measured dimensions (e.g. length × width × height). A sinking irregular solid has no simple shape, so its volume is instead found from the rise in a measuring cylinder's reading once it is fully submerged.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: A larger object always has a greater density simply because it is larger.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Learners often associate 'more' or 'bigger' with 'denser', especially when comparing a small and a large object by eye.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner predicts which of two objects is denser from their size alone, without calculating mass divided by volume for each.
misconceptions.correct_model: Density compares mass to volume together. Two objects of the same material have the same density whatever their size, because both their mass and their volume scale up together.
misconceptions.remediation: Compare two cubes of the same material but different sizes, calculate the density of each, and show the two results are equal.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: The total volume of the container is used as the object's volume.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: A measuring cylinder's scale shows the volume of whatever is inside it, so it is tempting to read off a single number without asking what that number actually represents.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner uses the measuring cylinder's total capacity (the top mark of its scale) as the volume of a liquid instead of reading the level at the bottom of the meniscus, or uses the final cylinder reading alone as a submerged solid's volume.
misconceptions.correct_model: Only the volume of the object itself counts. For a liquid, the volume is the level read at the bottom of the meniscus, not the cylinder's full capacity; for a submerged solid, the object's volume is the rise in the reading, not the final reading on its own.
misconceptions.remediation: Before calculating, ask: does this reading include something other than the object itself? If so, subtract that part first.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: The reading taken from water displacement gives the solid's mass.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Displacement and mass are both found using numbers from laboratory apparatus, so the two measurements can be confused as being the same kind of quantity.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner treats the rise in the measuring-cylinder reading as a mass value, or substitutes it directly for mass in a density calculation.
misconceptions.correct_model: Displacement gives a volume (in cm³), found from the rise in the liquid level. The mass of the solid must be measured separately with a balance; the two measurements are then combined as density = mass ÷ volume.
misconceptions.remediation: Label each number as it is produced: 'rise in cylinder reading = volume (cm³)', 'balance reading = mass (g)', before combining them.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using a container's full mass or volume reading instead of isolating the liquid or solid's own reading.
common_mistakes.why: The number on a scale always includes everything that contributed to it, not just the part of interest.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Subtract whatever does not belong to the object itself before using a reading in a density calculation.

common_mistakes.mistake: Treating the displaced-water reading as the solid's mass rather than its volume.
common_mistakes.why: Both numbers come from laboratory apparatus, which can make them feel interchangeable.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Label each quantity as it is produced: a rise in a cylinder reading is a volume, and a balance reading is a mass.

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming a bigger object is automatically denser.
common_mistakes.why: Density compares mass to volume together; both scale up with size for the same material, so their ratio stays the same.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Calculate mass divided by volume for each object before comparing them, rather than judging by size alone.

common_mistakes.mistake: Mixing g/cm³ and kg/m³ without converting between them.
common_mistakes.why: The two unit pairs differ by a factor of 1000, so comparing raw numbers from each gives a meaningless result.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Convert both densities to the same unit pair before comparing or combining them.

common_mistakes.mistake: Reading a measuring cylinder's final level without checking the irregular solid is completely covered by the liquid.
common_mistakes.why: A solid that is only partly submerged displaces less liquid than its true volume, so the calculated density comes out too high.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Confirm the solid is fully underwater, with no trapped air bubbles, before recording the final reading.

exam_notes: Always show the subtraction step explicitly, such as mass of liquid = full reading minus empty reading.
State the unit at every step, not only in the final answer.
For a displacement method, state that the solid must be completely submerged and free of trapped air bubbles.
When comparing or converting densities, show the ×1000 or ÷1000 step between g/cm³ and kg/m³ explicitly.

summary.big_idea: Density is a ratio of measured mass to measured volume, and the right method for finding that volume depends on whether the sample is a liquid, a regular solid or a sinking irregular solid.
key_points: Density is defined as $\rho=m/V$, with mass and volume in matching units.
For a liquid, subtract the empty-container mass before dividing by its volume.
For a regular solid, calculate the volume from its measured dimensions.
For a sinking irregular solid, use the rise in a measuring cylinder's reading, and only once it is fully submerged with no trapped air bubbles.
Convert between g/cm³ and kg/m³ using the factor 1000 before comparing densities given in different units.
summary.what_to_remember_if_nothing_else: Density always compares an object's own mass to its own volume, found with the method that matches its shape: direct reading for a liquid, calculation from dimensions for a regular solid, and displacement for a sinking irregular solid.

03_Density_and_floating.json.title: Density and floating
03_Density_and_floating.json.subject: Physics

objectives.statement: Use the density of an object and the density of a fluid to predict whether the object floats or sinks in that fluid.
Explain a floating or sinking prediction using measured or calculated density, in matching units, rather than mass alone.

prerequisites.statement: Calculate density as mass divided by volume, with consistent units (from the previous lesson on measuring density).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Every floating/sinking prediction in this lesson is a comparison of two densities, so each one must already be found or given correctly.

prerequisites.statement: Convert a density between g/cm³ and kg/m³ using the factor 1000.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Several comparisons in this lesson give the object and the fluid in different units, so they cannot be compared until one is converted to match the other.

prerequisites.statement: Compare two decimal numbers to determine which is larger.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: The floating/sinking rule is ultimately a comparison of two numbers, so this simple skill underlies every prediction in the lesson.

diagnostic_items.question: A metal has a density of 8900 kg/m³. Express this density in g/cm³, and state whether it is greater or less than the density of water, 1.0 g/cm³.

common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner multiplies by 1000 instead of dividing, converting in the wrong direction.
The learner changes the unit label without converting the number; the comparison with water then happens to come out right for the wrong reason.
The learner divides by 10 000, and so concludes wrongly that the metal is less dense than water and would float.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: This checks whether the learner can put two densities into the same unit pair, using $1\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}=1000\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}$, and then compare them; every prediction in this lesson rests on that comparison.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Write the conversion $1\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}=1000\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}$ at the top of the page, check the direction against the known pair (water is 1.0 g/cm³ and 1000 kg/m³), then repeat with one further value, for example 2700 kg/m³ giving 2.7 g/cm³.

theory_blocks.title: A massive log floats; a tiny nail sinks
theory_blocks.body:
A large log has a mass of 50 kg, far more than a small steel nail with a mass of 5.0 g, yet the log floats on water while the nail sinks straight to the bottom. Mass alone clearly cannot be what decides this, since the much more massive object is the one that floats.

The log's volume is also large: about $0.10\,\mathrm{m^3}$, which is $100\,000\,\mathrm{cm^3}$. Its density is $50\,000\div100\,000=0.5\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}$, less than water's density of $1.0\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}$. The nail's volume is tiny, only $0.64\,\mathrm{cm^3}$, giving a density of $5.0\div0.64\approx7.8\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}$, much greater than water's. What decides floating or sinking is [[blue:this ratio of mass to volume, the density]], compared with the density of the fluid, not the mass or the size on its own.

assets.caption: Mass alone is misleading: the far more massive log floats because its density (0.5 g/cm³) is lower than water's, while the tiny nail sinks because its density (about 7.8 g/cm³) is higher.
assets.purpose: Density comparison cards contrasting a large, low-density floating object with a small, high-density sinking object, directly countering the 'large mass sinks' misconception.

theory_blocks.title: Floating, sinking and neutral buoyancy
Comparing densities in the same units
theory_blocks.body:
Before comparing two densities, check that they are given in the same unit pair. If one is in g/cm³ and the other is in kg/m³, convert one to match the other using $1\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}=1000\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}$.

For example, a solid of density $2700\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}$ compared with water of density $1000\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}$: both are already in kg/m³, so $2700>1000$ and the solid sinks. The same solid compared with water quoted as $1.0\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}$ needs converting first: $2700\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}=2.7\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}$, and $2.7>1.0$, giving the same conclusion. Comparing 2700 directly against 1.0 without converting would wrongly suggest the solid is far denser than it actually is relative to water, and, worse, invites comparing numbers that do not mean the same thing.

theory_blocks.title: Hollow objects and overall density
theory_blocks.body:
A hollow object can have a low overall density even if the material it is made from is much denser than water. A hollow plastic ball with a total mass of 45 g and a total volume, including the trapped air inside, of 50 cm³ has an overall density of $45\div50=0.9\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}$, which floats, even though the solid plastic of its shell alone has a density of around $1.2\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}$, denser than water.

What matters for floating is the object's [[blue:**overall (mean) density**]], mass divided by its total volume including any enclosed air, not the density of the solid material it happens to be made from. This idea stays qualitative here: it does not require a separate buoyancy-force equation, only the same density comparison already used throughout this lesson, applied to the object as a whole.

keywords.definition: An object floats in a fluid when its density is lower than the fluid's density.
An object sinks in a fluid when its density is higher than the fluid's density.
Describes an object whose density exactly equals the fluid's density, so it stays suspended at any depth.
The total mass of an object divided by its total volume, including any enclosed air; this is what determines floating for a hollow object.

worked_examples.statement: **A straightforward prediction.** A block of wax has a density of 0.96 g/cm³. Water has a density of 1.00 g/cm³. Predict whether the wax floats or sinks in water, and justify your prediction.
worked_examples.solution: $0.96<1.00$, so the wax floats in water.
worked_examples.interpretation: The wax's density is lower than water's, so by the floating/sinking rule it floats; no information about the wax's mass or size on its own is needed.

worked_examples.statement: **Comparing in matching units.** A metal alloy has a density of 2700 kg/m³. Predict whether it floats or sinks in water, which has a density of 1000 kg/m³ (equivalently 1.0 g/cm³).
reasoning: Both densities are already given in kg/m³, so no conversion is actually needed here.
worked_examples.solution: $2700>1000$, so the alloy sinks in water.
worked_examples.interpretation: Expressed the other way, $2700\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}=2.7\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}$, and $2.7>1.0$, giving the same conclusion whichever matching unit pair is used.

worked_examples.statement: **Mass versus density.** A large log has a mass of 50 kg and a volume of 0.10 m³. A small steel nail has a mass of 5.0 g and a volume of 0.64 cm³. Show, using density, why the log floats in water while the nail sinks, even though the log is far more massive.
reasoning: Convert the log's measurements to matching units: $50\,\mathrm{kg}=50\,000\,\mathrm{g}$ and $0.10\,\mathrm{m^3}=100\,000\,\mathrm{cm^3}$.
Calculate each object's density separately, then compare each one with water's density of $1.0\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}$.
worked_examples.solution: Log: $\rho=50\,000\div100\,000=0.5\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}$, which is less than 1.0, so it floats. Nail: $\rho=5.0\div0.64\approx7.8\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}$, which is greater than 1.0, so it sinks.
worked_examples.interpretation: The log's much larger mass is matched by an even larger volume, giving a low density; the nail's tiny mass is packed into an even smaller volume, giving a high density. Density, not mass, decides the outcome.

worked_examples.statement: **A hollow object.** A hollow plastic ball has a total mass of 45 g and a total volume, including the trapped air inside, of 50 cm³. The solid plastic of its shell alone has a density of 1.2 g/cm³, which is greater than water's density of 1.0 g/cm³. Explain, with a calculation, whether the ball floats or sinks in water.
reasoning: The relevant density for floating is the ball's overall density, using its total mass and its total volume including the enclosed air, not the density of the solid shell material alone.
worked_examples.solution: Overall density $=45\div50=0.9\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}$. Since $0.9<1.0$, the ball floats.
worked_examples.interpretation: Even though the shell material itself (1.2 g/cm³) would sink on its own, the air trapped inside lowers the ball's overall mean density below water's, so the whole ball floats.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Comparing the shell material's density (1.2 g/cm³) with water and concluding the ball sinks, instead of using the ball's overall density including the enclosed air.

guided_exercises.statement: An object has a density of 1.05 g/cm³. It is placed in a liquid of density 1.20 g/cm³. Will the object float or sink? Justify your answer with an inequality.
hints: Compare the object's density with the liquid's density, in the same units.
A lower density than the surrounding liquid means the object floats.
Write the comparison as an inequality before stating your conclusion.
guided_exercises.answer: $1.05\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}<1.20\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}$, so the object floats in this liquid.
common_errors: Concluding the object sinks because 1.05 'feels close to' 1.20, instead of comparing the two values directly.
guided_exercises.full_solution:
**Step 1 — Identify:** Compare the object's density with the liquid's density, in the same units.

**Step 2 — Method:** A lower density than the surrounding liquid means the object floats.

**Step 3 — Calculate:** $1.05\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}<1.20\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}$, so the object floats in this liquid.

**Step 4 — Check:** Write the comparison as an inequality before stating your conclusion.

guided_exercises.statement: A solid has a density of 3100 kg/m³. Sea water has a density of 1.03 g/cm³. Will the solid float or sink in sea water?
hints: Convert both densities to the same units before comparing.
$1\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}=1000\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}$.
Compare the two values in kg/m³ and write the inequality.
guided_exercises.answer: $1.03\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}=1030\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}$. Since $3100\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}>1030\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}$, the solid sinks in sea water.
common_errors: Comparing 3100 directly with 1.03 without converting to the same units first.
guided_exercises.full_solution:
**Step 1 — Identify:** Convert both densities to the same units before comparing.

**Step 2 — Method:** $1\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}=1000\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}$.

**Step 3 — Calculate:** $1.03\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}=1030\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}$. Since $3100\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}>1030\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}$, the solid sinks in sea water.

**Step 4 — Check:** Compare the two values in kg/m³ and write the inequality.

exercises.statement: An ice cube has a density of 0.92 g/cm³. Predict whether it floats or sinks in water (density 1.00 g/cm³), giving a reason.
exercises.answer: $0.92<1.00$, so the ice cube floats in water.

exercises.statement: A rock has a density of 2.4 g/cm³, and vegetable oil has a density of 0.92 g/cm³. Predict whether the rock floats or sinks in the oil.
exercises.answer: $2.4>0.92$, so the rock sinks in the oil.

exercises.statement: A beach ball has a mass of 150 g and a volume of 6000 cm³, while a small steel ball bearing has a mass of 30 g and a volume of 3.8 cm³. (a) Calculate the density of each. (b) State which one floats in water and explain why predicting from mass alone would have given the wrong answer.
exercises.answer: (a) Beach ball: $150\div6000=0.025\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}$. Steel ball: $30\div3.8\approx7.9\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}$. (b) The beach ball floats ($0.025<1.00$) and the steel ball sinks ($7.9>1.00$), even though the beach ball has the larger mass: floating depends on density, mass per unit volume, not on mass by itself.
common_errors: Predicting that the heavier beach ball (150 g, versus 30 g for the ball bearing) is the one that sinks.

exercises.statement: A ship made of steel, which has a density of about 7900 kg/m³, floats in sea water. Explain, in terms of overall density, how a ship made from a material much denser than water can still float.
exercises.answer: A ship is not a solid lump of steel: its hull encloses a large volume of air inside. The ship's overall density, its total mass divided by its total volume, including the air enclosed by the hull, is lower than the density of sea water, even though the steel itself is far denser than water.
common_errors: Comparing only the density of steel with water and concluding that a steel ship must sink.

exam_questions.statement: Two liquids, A and B, do not mix. Liquid A has a density of 0.80 g/cm³ and liquid B, which is denser, settles at the bottom with a density of 1.10 g/cm³. A solid ball has a density of 0.95 g/cm³. Predict what happens when the ball is dropped into the container, and explain your answer.
exam_questions.answer: The ball's density (0.95 g/cm³) is greater than liquid A's density (0.80 g/cm³), so the ball sinks through liquid A. The ball's density is less than liquid B's density (1.10 g/cm³), so the ball floats once it reaches liquid B. The ball therefore comes to rest floating at the boundary between the two liquids.
mark_scheme: Compares the ball's density with liquid A's density and concludes the ball sinks through A.
Compares the ball's density with liquid B's density and concludes the ball floats on B.
States that the ball settles at the interface between the two liquids.
Gives both comparisons as explicit inequalities using the stated densities.

exam_questions.statement: A sample of rock has a mass of 212 g and a volume of 80 cm³. Sea water has a density of 1030 kg/m³. (a) Calculate the density of the rock in kg/m³. (b) Predict whether the rock floats or sinks in sea water, justifying your answer with a comparison of densities in the same units.
exam_questions.answer: (a) $\rho=212\div80=2.65\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}=2650\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}$. (b) Since $2650\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}>1030\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}$, the rock sinks in sea water.
mark_scheme: Uses density = mass ÷ volume, $212\div80$ (M1); $=2.65\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}$ (A1).
Converts this to $2650\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}$.
States the comparison $2650\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}>1030\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}$ explicitly.
Concludes correctly that the rock sinks, consistent with that comparison.

challenge_questions.statement: A sealed hollow steel sphere has an outer volume of 1000 cm³, including the air trapped inside, and its steel shell has a mass of 950 g. Water has a density of 1.00 g/cm³ and vegetable oil has a density of 0.92 g/cm³. (a) Calculate the overall density of the sphere. (b) Predict whether the sphere floats or sinks in water, and whether it floats or sinks in the oil, justifying each prediction. (c) Steel has a density of 7.9 g/cm³. Calculate the volume of steel in the shell, and hence the volume of air sealed inside the sphere.
hints: For part (a) use the whole sphere: its total mass divided by its total volume, including the trapped air.
For part (b) compare that one overall density with each fluid density in turn; the two comparisons need not give the same answer.
For part (c) rearrange $\rho=\dfrac{m}{V}$ to $V=\dfrac{m}{\rho}$ for the steel alone, then subtract that volume from the sphere's outer volume.
challenge_questions.answer: (a) Overall density $=950\div1000=0.95\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}$. (b) In water, $0.95<1.00$, so the sphere floats. In the oil, $0.95>0.92$, so the same sphere sinks. (c) Volume of steel $=950\div7.9\approx120\,\mathrm{cm^3}$, so the volume of air $\approx1000-120=880\,\mathrm{cm^3}$.
challenge_questions.full_solution: The sphere's overall density lies between the two fluid densities, which is why one object gives two different outcomes: floating is never a property of the object alone, only of the object compared with the fluid it is placed in. Part (c) shows why the overall density is so low: only about 120 cm³ of the 1000 cm³ is steel, and the remaining 880 cm³ of trapped air adds volume without adding appreciable mass.
common_errors: Comparing the density of steel, 7.9 g/cm³, with each fluid and concluding that the sphere sinks in both, instead of using the sphere's overall density of 0.95 g/cm³.
Assuming that an object which floats in water must float in every liquid, and so missing that the oil is less dense than the sphere.
Dividing by the steel density the wrong way round in part (c), $7.9\div950$, which gives a volume far smaller than the sphere itself.

mcq.stem: A block has a density of 0.78 g/cm³. Which of these liquids will the block float in?

options.why_wrong: this liquid is less dense than the block ($0.78>0.60$), so the block would sink in it, not float.
this liquid is still slightly less dense than the block ($0.78>0.75$), so the block would still sink.

options.text: A liquid of density $0.78\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}$, exactly equal to the block's
options.why_wrong: equal densities make the block neutrally buoyant, remaining suspended, not floating at the surface.

mcq.explanation: The block floats only in a liquid denser than itself. $0.78<1.00$, so option A is denser than the block and the block floats in it; option D gives equal densities, which means neutral buoyancy rather than floating at the surface.

mcq.stem: A liquid has a density of 850 kg/m³, and an object has a density of 0.90 g/cm³. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The object floats, because 0.90 is a smaller number than 850.
options.why_wrong: this compares the two numbers directly without converting them to the same units first, which is not a valid comparison.

options.text: The object floats, because $850\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}$ is greater than $0.90\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}$.
options.why_wrong: this is the same unit-mismatch error: comparing numbers given in different unit systems without converting them.

options.text: The object sinks, because $900\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}$ is greater than $850\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}$.
There is not enough information to decide.
options.why_wrong: both densities are given; converting one to match the other's units is enough to decide.

mcq.stem: Object X has a density exactly equal to the density of the liquid it is placed in. What happens to X?

options.text: X floats completely on the surface.
options.why_wrong: floating fully on the surface happens when X is less dense than the liquid, not when the two densities are equal.

options.text: X sinks straight to the bottom.
options.why_wrong: sinking to the bottom happens when X is denser than the liquid, not when the two densities are equal.
a density comparison predicts floating or sinking behaviour, not dissolving, which is an unrelated process.

options.text: X remains suspended at whatever depth it is placed, neither rising nor sinking further.

mcq.explanation: Equal densities give neutral buoyancy: the object stays suspended at any depth, neither floating up nor sinking further.

mcq.stem: Which comparison correctly predicts that an object sinks in a given liquid?

options.why_wrong: comparing the total masses of unspecified amounts of each says nothing about density, which depends on the ratio of mass to volume.
this is the condition for floating, the opposite of sinking.
comparing volumes alone, with no reference to mass, gives no information about density.

mcq.explanation: An object sinks when its density is greater than the surrounding liquid's density.

flashcards.front: What determines whether an object floats, sinks or stays suspended in a fluid?
flashcards.back: Comparing the object's density with the fluid's density: lower density floats, higher density sinks, equal density stays neutrally suspended.

flashcards.front: What must be true of two densities before they can be compared?
flashcards.back: They must be expressed in the same unit pair (both g/cm³ or both kg/m³); convert using $1\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}=1000\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}$ if they are not.

flashcards.front: Does a heavier object always sink?
flashcards.back: No. Floating and sinking depend on density, mass per unit volume, not on mass alone; a massive object can still have a low density and float.

flashcards.front: Why does a large log float while a small steel nail sinks, even though the log has far more mass?
flashcards.back: The log's volume is large enough that its density (about 0.5 g/cm³) is below water's; the nail's volume is so small that its density (about 7.8 g/cm³) is well above water's. Density, not mass, decides the outcome.

flashcards.front: How can a hollow object made of a material denser than water still float?
flashcards.back: Its overall density, total mass divided by total volume including any enclosed air, can be lower than water's even though the solid material of its shell alone is denser than water.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Any object with a large mass sinks.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: A heavy object is intuitively associated with sinking, and in everyday experience small light objects often do float.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner predicts sinking from a large mass value alone, without calculating or comparing density.
misconceptions.correct_model: Floating and sinking depend on density, mass per unit volume, not on mass by itself. A massive object with a large enough volume can have a lower density than the fluid, and float, while a small object made of a very dense material can sink.
misconceptions.remediation: Compare a large, low-density object with a small, high-density object directly, calculating the density of each before predicting which floats.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Densities given in different units can be compared directly, without converting them first.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Both numbers look like ordinary decimals, so it is tempting to compare them as they are printed, without checking what unit each one carries.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner compares a density in g/cm³ directly against one in kg/m³, for example treating 0.90 as smaller than 850 without converting either value.
misconceptions.correct_model: Densities must be expressed in the same unit pair before comparing them. Convert g/cm³ to kg/m³ by multiplying by 1000, or the reverse by dividing by 1000, then compare.
misconceptions.remediation: Before comparing, check the unit on each density; if they differ, convert one so that both share the same unit.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Equal densities mean the object sinks immediately.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Learners expect every comparison to have a clear winner, and may assume a tie defaults to sinking.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner states that an object sinks to the bottom when its density exactly equals the fluid's density.
misconceptions.correct_model: When an object's density equals the fluid's density, it is neutrally buoyant: it remains suspended at whatever depth it is placed, neither rising to the surface nor sinking further.
misconceptions.remediation: Contrast the three cases explicitly: lower density floats, higher density sinks, equal density stays suspended.

common_mistakes.mistake: Predicting floating or sinking from mass alone instead of density.
common_mistakes.why: A larger mass is often assumed to mean 'heavier relative to the fluid', but floating depends on mass per unit volume, not mass by itself.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Always calculate or compare density, not mass, before predicting floating or sinking.

common_mistakes.mistake: Comparing densities given in different units without converting them first.
common_mistakes.why: Numbers in g/cm³ and kg/m³ differ by a factor of 1000, so comparing the raw figures gives a meaningless result.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Convert one density so that both are in the same unit pair before comparing.

common_mistakes.mistake: Treating equal densities as meaning the object sinks immediately.
common_mistakes.why: Equal densities actually give neutral buoyancy, not sinking.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Remember the three distinct outcomes: lower density floats, higher density sinks, equal density stays suspended.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using the density of a hollow object's solid material instead of its overall density.
common_mistakes.why: The trapped air inside a hollow object lowers its overall density below that of the solid material alone.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: For a hollow object, use its total mass divided by its total volume, including any enclosed air, not the density of the material it is made from.

exam_notes: State both densities being compared, in the same units, before giving a floats/sinks conclusion.
Convert g/cm³ to kg/m³ (×1000) or the reverse (÷1000) and show this step explicitly if the two densities are given in different units.
Name the specific liquid or fluid used in the comparison; 'it floats' alone is not a complete answer.
For a hollow object, refer to its overall (mean) density, not the density of the solid material it is made from.

summary.big_idea: An object floats or sinks according to its density relative to the density of the fluid it is placed in, not according to its mass alone.
key_points: Compare the object's density with the fluid's density: lower floats, higher sinks, equal stays neutrally suspended.
Convert densities to the same unit pair (g/cm³ or kg/m³, using the factor 1000) before comparing them.
A massive object can still float if its volume is large enough to give it a low density; a tiny object can still sink if its density is high.
A hollow object's floating depends on its overall density, including any enclosed air, not on the density of the solid material it is made from.
summary.what_to_remember_if_nothing_else: Compare densities, in matching units, not masses: lower than the fluid floats, higher than the fluid sinks.

summary.big_idea: Use the key physics ideas and methods from mass weight and density accurately in mixed practice and exam-style problems.

exercises.statement: A body of mass 1 kg has weight 10 N at a certain place. What is the weight of (a) 100 g (b) 5 kg (c) 50 g?
exercises.full_solution: At this place, 1 kg weighs 10 N, so the weight per unit mass (the local gravitational field strength, $g$) is 10 N/kg. Using $W = mg$, first convert each mass to kilograms, then multiply by 10 N/kg. (a) 100 g = 0.1 kg, so $W = 0.1 \times 10 = 1$ N. (b) 5 kg is already in kg, so $W = 5 \times 10 = 50$ N. (c) 50 g = 0.05 kg, so $W = 0.05 \times 10 = 0.5$ N.

exercises.statement: What does an astronaut of mass 100 kg weigh (a) on Earth where the gravitational field strength is 10 N/kg (b) on the Moon where the gravitational field strength is 1.6 N/kg?
exercises.full_solution: Mass does not change with location, but weight depends on the local gravitational field strength $g$ through $W = mg$. (a) On Earth: $W = 100 \text{ kg} \times 10 \text{ N/kg} = 1000$ N. (b) On the Moon: $W = 100 \text{ kg} \times 1.6 \text{ N/kg} = 160$ N. The astronaut's weight on the Moon is much less than on Earth (about one-sixth) even though their mass (amount of matter) is unchanged.

exercises.statement: (a) If the density of wood is 0.5 g/cm³, what is the mass of (i) 1 cm³ (ii) 2 cm³ (iii) 10 cm³? (b) What is the density of a substance of (i) mass 100 g and volume 10 cm³ (ii) volume 3 m³ and mass 9 kg? (c) The density of gold is 19 g/cm³. Find the volume of (i) 38 g (ii) 95 g of gold.
exercises.answer: (a) (i) 0.5 g (ii) 1.0 g (iii) 5.0 g. (b) (i) 10 g/cm³ (ii) 3 kg/m³ (= 0.003 g/cm³). (c) (i) 2 cm³ (ii) 5 cm³
exercises.full_solution: Use $\rho = \frac{m}{V}$, rearranged as needed. (a) Mass $= \rho \times V$ with $\rho = 0.5$ g/cm³: (i) $0.5 \times 1 = 0.5$ g, (ii) $0.5 \times 2 = 1.0$ g, (iii) $0.5 \times 10 = 5.0$ g. (b)(i) $\rho = m/V = 100 \text{ g} / 10 \text{ cm}^3 = 10$ g/cm³. (b)(ii) $\rho = m/V = 9 \text{ kg} / 3 \text{ m}^3 = 3$ kg/m³; converting (divide by 1000 to go from kg/m³ to g/cm³) this is $3/1000 = 0.003$ g/cm³ — note this is a very low density (only about twice that of air, 1.3 kg/m³, so it would have to be a gas or a very light foam), but it follows correctly from the numbers given. (c) $V = m/\rho$ with $\rho = 19$ g/cm³: (i) $38/19 = 2$ cm³, (ii) $95/19 = 5$ cm³.

exercises.statement: A piece of steel has a volume of 12 cm³ and a mass of 96 g. What is its density in (a) g/cm³ (b) kg/m³?
exercises.full_solution: (a) $\rho = m/V = 96 \text{ g} / 12 \text{ cm}^3 = 8$ g/cm³. (b) To convert g/cm³ to kg/m³, multiply by 1000 (since 1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³): $8 \times 1000 = 8000$ kg/m³. This is a sensible value for steel, which is slightly denser than iron (table value 7.9 g/cm³ = 7900 kg/m³) given in the book.

exercises.statement: What is the mass of 5 m³ of cement of density 3000 kg/m³?
exercises.full_solution: Use $m = V \times \rho = 5 \text{ m}^3 \times 3000 \text{ kg/m}^3 = 15\,000$ kg. This is a large but realistic figure for a 5 m³ block of solid cement (15 tonnes).

exercises.statement: What is the mass of air in a room measuring 10 m × 5.0 m × 2.0 m if the density of air is 1.3 kg/m³?
exercises.full_solution: First find the volume of the room: $V = 10 \times 5.0 \times 2.0 = 100$ m³. Then use $m = V \times \rho = 100 \text{ m}^3 \times 1.3 \text{ kg/m}^3 = 130$ kg. This is a plausible mass for the air filling a typical room of that size.

exercises.statement: When a golf ball is lowered into a measuring cylinder of water, the water level rises by 30 cm³ when the ball is completely submerged. If the ball weighs 33 g in air, find its density.
